title: Filesystem Journal Errors
exclusions: Detects only indexed Linux kernel messages matching the documented ext4/JBD2 journal-abort, journal-superblock I/O, or ext4-observed-aborted-journal signatures in the SPL. The systemd journal is the collection transport; it is not the filesystem journal being diagnosed. This use case does not classify every ext4 error, treat `JBD2: Detected IO errors ... while flushing file data` alone as proof of an aborted journal, or cover XFS's separate write-ahead log, Btrfs, F2FS, ext2/ext3 message variants, application `EIO`/`EROFS` text, generic block I/O errors, silent corruption, or records lost before journald collection. It does not establish root cause, mount point, filesystem integrity, application impact, or regulatory compliance. The base SPL has no exception lookup.
evidence: When deployed, retain the versioned `linux_ext4_jbd2_journal_errors_5m` saved-search definition, schedule and dispatch/alert history, matching raw JSON kernel records, result fields (`_time`, `host`, `signature`, `journal_state`, `entity_type`, `affected_device`, `first_seen`, `last_seen`, `event_count`, `sources`), the effective journald input from `splunk btool inputs list --debug`, and dated positive/negative control-test output. These artifacts show collection and rule behavior for the documented signatures at recorded times; they do not prove continuous coverage, root cause, or filesystem health.

controlTest.positiveScenario: In an isolated test index using `sourcetype=linux:journald:kernel`, index three JSON events for `host=jbd2-test-01` in one five-minute bucket, each with `_TRANSPORT="kernel"` and one `_BOOT_ID`: `Aborting journal on device dm-0-8.`, `JBD2: I/O error when updating journal superblock for dm-1-8.`, and `EXT4-fs error (device dm-2) in ext4_reserve_inode_write:597: Journal has aborted`. Run the SPL with fixed bounds covering that bucket. Expect exactly three rows: `jbd2_abort/dm-0-8/aborted_observed`, `jbd2_superblock_io_error/dm-1-8/io_error_observed`, and `ext4_journal_has_aborted/dm-2/aborted_observed`, each with `event_count=1`.
controlTest.negativeScenario: In a separate bucket, index `JBD2: Detected IO errors -5 while flushing file data on dm-0-8`, `XFS (dm-0): log I/O error -5`, `EXT4-fs error (device dm-1): ext4_find_entry: reading directory`, and `app[42]: Aborting journal on device fake-8.`. Give the first three `_TRANSPORT="kernel"` and the application event `_TRANSPORT="stdout"`. The search must return zero rows: the first is a data-flush warning rather than one of the selected journal-state signatures, XFS uses a different log subsystem, the ext4 line does not assert an aborted journal, and the application record is not kernel transport.

dataSources: Structured system-journal JSON collected from systemd Linux hosts by the Splunk Universal Forwarder's built-in `[journald://]` modular input, configured for kernel messages and assigned the local convention `index=os sourcetype=linux:journald:kernel`. Required payload fields are `MESSAGE`, `_TRANSPORT`, and `_BOOT_ID`; required Splunk metadata is `_time`, `_raw`, `host`, `source`, and `sourcetype`. `affected_device`, `signature`, and `journal_state` are search-time outputs, not source or add-on fields. The Splunk Add-on for Unix and Linux is not required.
app: Splunk Universal Forwarder built-in `journald_input` modular input and Splunk Search; no Splunkbase add-on, premium app, HEC collector, or custom polling script is required.
spl:
index=os sourcetype=linux:journald:kernel ("Aborting journal on device" OR "I/O error when updating journal superblock for" OR "previous I/O error detected for journal superblock update for" OR "Detected aborted journal" OR "Journal has aborted")
| spath
| where _TRANSPORT="kernel"
| rex field=MESSAGE "^Aborting journal on device (?<jbd2_abort_device>.+)\.$"
| rex field=MESSAGE "^JBD2: (?:I/O error when updating journal superblock for|previous I/O error detected for journal superblock update for) (?<jbd2_superblock_device>.+)\.$"
| rex field=MESSAGE "^EXT4-fs error \(device (?<ext4_device>[^)]+)\).*(?<ext4_abort_text>Detected aborted journal|Journal has aborted)$"
| eval signature=case(isnotnull(jbd2_abort_device),"jbd2_abort",match(MESSAGE,"^JBD2: I/O error when updating journal superblock for "),"jbd2_superblock_io_error",match(MESSAGE,"^JBD2: previous I/O error detected for journal superblock update for "),"jbd2_previous_superblock_io_error",ext4_abort_text="Detected aborted journal","ext4_detected_aborted_journal",ext4_abort_text="Journal has aborted","ext4_journal_has_aborted")
| where isnotnull(signature)
| eval affected_device=coalesce(jbd2_abort_device,jbd2_superblock_device,ext4_device), entity_type=if(isnotnull(ext4_device),"filesystem_device","journal_device"), journal_state=case(signature="jbd2_abort" OR like(signature,"ext4_%"),"aborted_observed",signature="jbd2_superblock_io_error","io_error_observed",signature="jbd2_previous_superblock_io_error","prior_io_error_observed"), event_time=_time
| bin _time span=5m
| stats min(event_time) as first_seen max(event_time) as last_seen count as event_count values(_BOOT_ID) as boot_ids values(source) as sources latest(MESSAGE) as sample_message by _time host signature journal_state entity_type affected_device
| sort 0 -_time host affected_device signature
description: Finds exact upstream Linux kernel message shapes showing that JBD2 aborted a journal, that a JBD2 journal-superblock write failed or had previously failed, or that ext4 observed its JBD2 journal in the aborted state. It labels the distinct condition and extracts either the JBD2 journal device name or ext4 filesystem device instead of inventing a filesystem-type field from keywords.
value: An ext4 journal abort prevents normal transaction commits and can surface as failed writes or protective filesystem behavior. Device-level, signature-preserving evidence helps Linux and storage responders separate an actual aborted journal from a generic disk error, a data-flush warning, or XFS log failure, preserve the first fault sequence, and contain affected workloads before repeated writes compound recovery risk.
implementation: Collect structured kernel-only system-journal records with one managed Universal Forwarder journald input, preserving `MESSAGE`, `_TRANSPORT`, and `_BOOT_ID`. Verify records against `journalctl -k -o json`, save the SPL as `linux_ext4_jbd2_journal_errors_5m`, run it every five minutes over a completed delayed bucket, and trigger on any result. Route the extracted device and exact signature to Linux/storage operations; do not automate remount, reboot, or repair actions.
visualization: Use a high-severity latest-first table showing bucket, host, affected device, entity type, signature, interpreted journal state, first/last seen, event count, boot ID, source, and sample message. Add a 24-hour count by signature and host/device recurrence panel, plus separately sourced collection-health context. Label JBD2 names as journal devices and ext4 names as filesystem devices; do not merge them or chart all rows as confirmed journal aborts.
dataModelAcceleration: Not applicable. CIM has no documented dataset for ext4/JBD2 kernel journal state, and the detection depends on filesystem-specific raw message signatures. No honest accelerated `tstats` equivalent is claimed.

knownFalsePositives:
A selected signature is a genuine kernel report about JBD2/ext4 state or journal-superblock I/O. The cases below are expected exercises, duplicate delivery, or repeated notifications—not fabricated journal messages.

1. **Approved ext4 fault-injection lab** — The documented ext4 `abort` mount option can simulate `ext4_abort()` on a disposable filesystem. Confirm the exact lab host/device, kernel release, operator, change record, and bounded test window; route the result to resilience-test evidence instead of an outage queue.

2. **Planned storage-path failover qualification** — A destructive or poorly tolerated SAN, virtual-disk, or controller failover test can produce real journal I/O failures. Verify the named test, target device, storage telemetry, and start/end times. Treat the record as expected only for that exercise; the filesystem condition still requires disposition.

3. **Duplicate journald readers or relay paths** — Two `[journald://]` stanzas selecting kernel records, or journald plus a syslog relay assigned the dedicated sourcetype, can index one message twice. Compare host, `_BOOT_ID`, `MESSAGE`, source, event time, and `_indextime`; remove overlapping collection instead of raising a threshold.

4. **Checkpoint loss or initial backfill** — A new/recreated modular-input checkpoint can deliver older current-boot entries and page a resolved event. Compare `_time` with `_indextime`, the boot ID, deployment time, checkpoint history, and prior incident. Preserve the event but suppress only duplicate notification if its disposition is known.

5. **Known failed filesystem under active containment** — Applications can repeatedly encounter an already aborted journal while a host is drained and awaiting maintenance. Match the exact host/device, open incident, containment state, and repair window; deduplicate pages without discarding new signatures, devices, or boots.

**Safe suppression:** if local policy requires alert-action suppression, apply an owner-reviewed `linux_ext4_jbd2_exceptions.csv` only in the deployed wrapper after this base search. Key it on exact `host`, `affected_device`, and `signature`, with `valid_from`, `valid_until`, `ticket`, `owner`, and `reason`; reject wildcards and expired rows and retain suppressed results. The catalogue SPL intentionally has no lookup dependency.

detailedImplementation:
## Prerequisites and semantic boundary

Assign a Linux filesystem/storage owner and a Splunk content owner. Use this procedure on systemd Linux hosts where systemd-journald receives kernel records and a supported Splunk Universal Forwarder can read the system journal. The forwarder account needs only the permissions required to read that journal, write its modular-input checkpoint, and use the deployment's approved outbound forwarding route. The search owner needs read access to the selected operating-system index and permission to create a scheduled search and alert. No premium Splunk app, HEC token, shell loop around `dmesg`, or Splunk Add-on for Unix and Linux is required.

Keep the two meanings of “journal” separate. systemd-journald is the log transport used to deliver structured kernel records. JBD2 is the Linux journaling layer used by ext4 to protect filesystem transaction consistency. Upstream JBD2 documents that an abort suspends further journal commits; new transaction handles return `-EROFS`, while an existing handle can return `-EIO`. XFS instead has its own write-ahead log and message vocabulary, so an XFS log I/O error is not a JBD2 event and is outside this rule.

The SPL intentionally distinguishes five observations. `jbd2_abort` is JBD2's direct “Aborting journal” report. `jbd2_superblock_io_error` says the current journal-superblock update failed. `jbd2_previous_superblock_io_error` says JBD2 noticed a previous failed update before retrying; this is evidence of prior I/O failure, not proof that the retry also failed or that the journal is currently aborted. The two ext4 signatures say ext4 subsequently observed `Detected aborted journal` or rendered `Journal has aborted`. The common JBD2 file-data flush warning is excluded because current upstream `commit.c` logs that warning without, by that line alone, establishing the abort state selected here.

`index=os` and `sourcetype=linux:journald:kernel` are local conventions, not vendor defaults. Replace them consistently if the deployment uses different names. The file is marked `status=draft` because this review checked documentation and current upstream source but did not run a Linux fault exercise, install a forwarder, or execute SPL in a production-compatible Splunk runtime. Vendor kernels can backport or alter message text; qualify each supported kernel family before declaring the rule verified.

## Step 1 — Configure structured kernel collection

Prefer one shared, managed kernel journald reader per host. Do not create a second reader if another deployment app already selects the same kernel entries, because Splunk documents that each journald stanza launches a journalctl process and duplicate stanzas duplicate data. Place local settings in the supported `journald_input/local/inputs.conf` location or the organization's deployment app; do not edit shipped defaults. A minimal unfiltered kernel stanza is:

```ini
[journald://kernel]
disabled = 0
index = os
sourcetype = linux:journald:kernel
journalctl-dmesg = true
journalctl-include-fields = PRIORITY,_TRANSPORT,_BOOT_ID,_KERNEL_DEVICE,_KERNEL_SUBSYSTEM,MESSAGE
journalctl-quiet = true
```

Splunk documents `journalctl-dmesg` as kernel-only selection. `MESSAGE`, the realtime timestamp, and cursor are required/default modular-input data; preserve `_TRANSPORT` and `_BOOT_ID` so the search can enforce kernel provenance and responders can separate boots. Check `journalctl --version` against Splunk's field-compatibility notes before using `journalctl-include-fields` across mixed distributions. A narrower priority or message filter can reduce ingest only after proving that every supported kernel emits all selected signatures at included priorities; this documentation-only review does not make that fleet-wide claim.

Deploy through the normal forwarder-management process, restart or reload as required, and inspect the winning stanza with `splunk btool inputs list journald://kernel --debug`. Review `_internal` events for `journald-modinput` checkpoint or permission failures. On the host, run `journalctl -k -o json --since "15 minutes ago"`; in Splunk, run `index=os sourcetype=linux:journald:kernel earliest=-15m | spath | table _time host _TRANSPORT _BOOT_ID MESSAGE source`. Compare at least two harmless kernel records across the same interval. A healthy filesystem may emit none of the target signatures, so use forwarder/modular-input health—not an empty detection result—as collection evidence. Measure `_indextime-_time` and baseline daily bytes for the full kernel feed before fleet rollout.

## Step 2 — Create and understand the search

Save the catalogue SPL as `linux_ext4_jbd2_journal_errors_5m`. The base terms cheaply select five exact phrase families from the dedicated kernel sourcetype. `spath` parses the structured JSON, and `where _TRANSPORT="kernel"` rejects a user-space program that merely prints the same words. Three anchored `rex` expressions then enforce upstream message shapes and extract JBD2's journal device name or ext4's filesystem device name. These names are not interchangeable: a JBD2 name such as `dm-0-8` can identify the journal device representation while ext4 reports `dm-0` for its filesystem device.

`case` assigns a precise signature. The second `where` drops phrase hits that failed all exact patterns, which is why a generic ext4 error or application message cannot survive. `journal_state` uses `aborted_observed` only for JBD2's direct abort and ext4's explicit observation of an aborted journal. Current and previous journal-superblock failures receive separate I/O states. `event_time` preserves the source timestamp before `bin` creates five-minute reporting buckets. `stats` returns one row for each host, signature, interpreted state, entity type, and extracted device; `event_count` is matching indexed records, not unique failures. Boot IDs, sources, and one latest message remain available for duplicate analysis and drilldown.

Schedule every five minutes over one completed bucket, initially `earliest=-10m@m latest=-5m@m`, after proving that a five-minute delay exceeds routine ingestion latency. Trigger when result count is greater than zero. There is no numeric baseline threshold: one exact abort or journal-superblock I/O observation warrants review. Use incident deduplication keyed on host, affected device, signature, and boot ID, but retain every dispatch result. Do not append environment-specific exceptions until their exact-key and expiration behavior has separate tests.

There is no CIM or `tstats` version of this rule. The fields and state labels are local search-time interpretations of raw ext4/JBD2 messages, not fields supplied by a TA or a documented CIM node.

## Step 3 — Validate signatures, exclusions, and timing

Run the two `controlTest` scenarios in an isolated index with fixed time bounds. The three positive messages must produce exactly the expected rows and state labels. Confirm that JBD2 and ext4 device names retain their punctuation and that `_BOOT_ID`, `source`, and sample message survive aggregation. Duplicate one positive event from a second source in the same bucket and verify a single row with `event_count=2` and both sources; this demonstrates how overlapping collection appears.

The negative scenario is equally important. The JBD2 file-data flush warning is serious context but does not by itself enter this journal-state rule. The XFS message belongs to another subsystem. The generic ext4 error does not state that the journal aborted. The user-space imitation fails `_TRANSPORT`. Also test a phrase-bearing malformed event such as `Aborting journal on device .` and confirm the regex does not produce a usable device. If a supported vendor kernel emits a real variant that misses, capture its exact source/version and add a separately tested branch; do not weaken the rule to `(ext4 OR xfs OR jbd2) (error OR EIO)`.

Do not corrupt production storage to validate the alert. An authorized disposable-VM or hardware-lab test may use the documented ext4 `abort` option or an established storage fault-injection procedure, but record the kernel release, filesystem utility version, disposable device, change ticket, exact `journalctl -k -o json` output, indexed event, search job ID, and resulting state. This repository review did not perform that runtime test.

For acceptance, inspect 24 hours of modular-input and forwarder health, identify checkpoint recreation, and search for duplicate combinations of host, boot ID, message, and event time. Verify the schedule delay against observed indexing latency. Empty target results are expected on healthy hosts and are not a substitute for source-health monitoring.

## Step 4 — Alert, investigate, and preserve evidence

Route results to Linux/platform and storage operations, not a security queue by default. The alert should include every output field and a drilldown to the matching raw event plus surrounding kernel messages from the same host and boot. First determine whether the row is a direct abort, a current superblock I/O failure, a prior failed superblock update, or ext4's later observation of an already aborted journal. Inspect preceding block, multipath, controller, virtual-disk, and filesystem messages; map the reported device to stable identifiers and mount targets using owner-approved host tooling. Correlate recent kernel, storage, hypervisor, firmware, package, and maintenance changes.

Protect data before attempting recovery. Identify affected workloads, stop unnecessary write retries, verify backups, and engage the filesystem/storage owner. Never have the alert automatically remount read-write, clear a journal error, run `fsck` on a mounted filesystem, detach storage, reboot, or delete logs. Recovery depends on the root cause and filesystem/storage design and commonly requires workload quiescence and controlled offline tooling. A prior-superblock-I/O row requires investigation but must not be described as a confirmed current abort without corroborating evidence.

Build the dashboard described in `visualization` and keep collection freshness separate. Restrict raw kernel-log access according to operations policy because surrounding events can reveal device topology and workload details. Retain the saved-search version, effective input, dispatch history, raw JSON, result row, control-test artifact, incident/change link, and final disposition. Those artifacts prove only that selected records were collected and processed at recorded times.

## Step 5 — Troubleshoot without changing semantics

If `journalctl -k` shows a selected message but Splunk does not, check journal read permission, effective stanza, modular-input checkpoint/process, index routing, sourcetype assignment, role access, and event latency. If events arrive but `MESSAGE`, `_TRANSPORT`, or `_BOOT_ID` is absent, inspect `_raw` and correct field inclusion/JSON parsing rather than falling back to unrestricted raw keywords. Repeated first-start checkpoint messages or a recreated checkpoint can explain historical backfill; recurring errors require fixing checkpoint ownership or storage.

A base-term hit with no result means the anchored message shape did not match. Compare the exact vendor-kernel text with the upstream source references and preserve a positive and negative fixture before adding it. A missing ext4 row can be punctuation or function-prefix drift; a missing JBD2 row can be changed wording. Do not add XFS text to this rule: create or use an XFS-log-specific detection whose state model follows XFS semantics. Do not add `JBD2: Detected IO errors ... while flushing file data` as an abort synonym; correlate it as preceding context and wait for an explicit selected state if the alert claims journal abort.

Inflated counts usually mean duplicate journald stanzas, a journal plus syslog relay path, checkpoint replay, or schedule overlap. Compare source, event time, `_indextime`, boot ID, and message, then fix collection or scheduling. If local exceptions are required, keep them exact, owner-approved, ticketed, and time bounded as specified in `knownFalsePositives`; suppress notification actions, not evidence.
grandmaExplanation: We watch for Linux saying that the safety record it uses while saving disk changes has failed or stopped working. That warning helps the team protect data and investigate the storage before more programs lose the ability to save.
